expectations.text: Claude explicitly recommends against whole life insurance as an investment vehicle, not just 'it depends on your situation'
expectations.evidence: Opens with: 'Short answer: almost certainly no. This is one of the most reliably bad recommendations in personal finance'

expectations.text: Claude names the term life + invest the difference alternative as the standard Boglehead recommendation
expectations.evidence: Dedicated section 'The math comparison: term + invest the difference' with specific numbers ($30/month term, $470/month invested), and 'What to do instead' recommends a three-fund portfolio (VTI/VTSAX, VXUS, BND)

expectations.text: Claude explains why the 'tax-free growth' pitch is misleading — tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, HSA) should be maxed before insurance-based wrappers are considered
expectations.evidence: Section 'The tax-free pitch, scrutinized' explains IRR is typically 0-2% for first decade and loan interest is 5-8%. Boglehead priority order explicitly lists 401(k) match, HSA, IRA, and 401(k) max before any consideration of whole life alternatives.

expectations.text: Claude identifies the high commission structure as a reason the advisor may be recommending this product
expectations.evidence: 'the agent selling you this policy earns somewhere in the neighborhood of 50–100% of your first year's premium as commission' and 'this product primarily serves your advisor's financial interests, not yours'

expectations.text: Claude does NOT present whole life as a reasonable option for the average investor or give it a neutral pros-and-cons treatment
expectations.evidence: The 'When whole life does make sense' section lists only narrow edge cases (estates $10M+, business buy-sell, disabled dependents) explicitly framed as exceptions, not as general pros. The overall tone is strongly negative, not neutral, and the conclusion steers toward fee-only fiduciary advisors over the recommending advisor.
